title: Printing Variables
summary: Combine text and variables with concatenation, printf, String.format, and formatted.
intro: Real output mixes fixed text with values from variables. Java gives you three tools for that: the `+` operator for quick lines, `printf` for precise formatting, and `String.format` or `formatted` when you want the formatted text as a String.

steps.title: Concatenation with +
steps.body:
When one side of `+` is a String, Java turns the other side into text and joins them. Numbers, chars, booleans, and doubles all work.

```java
String name = "Ada";
int level = 7;
System.out.println("Hi " + name + ", level " + level);   // Hi Ada, level 7
System.out.println("Online: " + true);                   // Online: true
```

The gotcha: `+` runs left to right. `"Total: " + 1` is already a String, so the next `+ 2` appends `2` as text instead of adding.

```java
System.out.println("Total: " + 1 + 2);    // Total: 12
System.out.println("Total: " + (1 + 2));  // Total: 3
```

Wrap math in parentheses so it happens first. Until a String shows up, `+` still does math: `1 + 2 + " items"` is `3 items`, and `'A' + 'B'` with no String at all is the number `131`. Also remember that spaces are not added for you: put them inside the quotes.

example.title: Player summary
example.prompt: Print a player summary built from five variables, then show the left-to-right gotcha next to its fix.
example.output:
Player Ada (rank B) is level 7
Health: 82.5, online: true
Total: 12
Total: 3
example.explanation: Each `+` with a String on one side turns the value into text: the char `B`, the int `7`, the double `82.5`, and the boolean `true`. In `"Total: " + 1 + 2` the first `+` makes `"Total: 1"`, so the second just appends `2`. The parentheses in `(1 + 2)` force the addition to happen first.

practice.title: Fruit basket
practice.prompt:
Print a fruit basket report using `+` concatenation.

1. Print `Fruit: 3 apples + 2 pears = 5` using `apples` and `pears`, and compute the total inside the line with `(apples + pears)`.
2. On the next line print `Basket weight: 1.25 kg, fresh: true` using `weight` and `fresh`.

Expected output:

```text
Fruit: 3 apples + 2 pears = 5
Basket weight: 1.25 kg, fresh: true
```

tests.output:
Fruit: 3 apples + 2 pears = 5
Basket weight: 1.25 kg, fresh: true

hints: Fixed text goes in quotes, variables go outside them: `"Fruit: " + apples + " apples"`.
Without parentheses, `... + apples + pears` prints `32` instead of `5`.

steps.title: printf format specifiers
steps.body:
`System.out.printf` takes a format string followed by values. Each `%` specifier is replaced by the next value, in order.

| Specifier | Prints | Example output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `%s` | a String (or any value as text) | `Ada` |
| `%d` | an int or long | `42` |
| `%f` | a double, 6 decimals | `3.500000` |
| `%.2f` | a double, 2 decimals | `3.50` |
| `%c` | a char | `M` |
| `%b` | a boolean | `true` |
| `%n` | a newline | |

A number before the letter sets a minimum width. By default the padding goes on the left (right aligned), and a `-` puts it on the right (left aligned). A longer value is never cut, it just pushes the line wider. That is how you line up columns.

```java
System.out.printf("[%5d] [%-8s] [%6.2f]%n", 42, "Ada", 3.5);
// [   42] [Ada     ] [  3.50]
```

`printf` does not end the line, so finish with `%n`. The type must match: `%d` needs an integer and `%f` a double. A mismatch such as `printf("%d", 2.5)` compiles but throws an exception when it runs.

example.title: Clothing table
example.prompt: Print two aligned rows of clothing items with printf, then show what plain %f prints.
example.output:
Shirt     19.50 M true
Jacket    74.00 L false
Plain f: 19.500000
example.explanation: `%-8s` pads each name to 8 characters on the right, so the prices start in the same column. `%6.2f` rounds to 2 decimals and right-aligns in 6 characters, which is why `19.50` gets one leading space. `%c` and `%b` print the char and boolean, and `%n` ends each row. Plain `%f` always shows 6 decimals.

practice.title: Stock table
practice.prompt:
Print an aligned table of three products with printf.

1. Use one `printf` per product, in the order Notebook, Backpack, Pen.
2. Print the name with `%-10s`, the quantity with `%3d`, the price with `%6.2f`, the size with `%c`, and inStock with `%b`, in that order.
3. Put one space between columns and end each row with `%n`.

Expected output:

```text
Notebook    12   3.49 A true
Backpack     3  45.00 L false
Pen        150   1.25 S true
```

tests.output:
Notebook    12   3.49 A true
Backpack     3  45.00 L false
Pen        150   1.25 S true

hints: Start each row with `System.out.printf(`, then the format string, then that product's five variables separated by commas.
`%3d` right-aligns the quantity in 3 characters, so `3` gets two leading spaces, and `%6.2f` gives `3.49` two.

steps.title: String.format and formatted
steps.body:
Sometimes you want the formatted text as a String to store or reuse, not printed right away. `String.format` takes the same format string as `printf` and returns the result. Java 15 also lets you call `formatted` on the format string itself, which reads a little shorter.

```java
String a = String.format("%s scored %d", "Ada", 90);
String b = "%s scored %d".formatted("Ada", 90);
System.out.println(a);   // Ada scored 90
```

Two more specifiers come up all the time:

- `%,d` adds thousands separators: `1234567` becomes `1,234,567`.
- `%%` prints a literal percent sign.

A lone `%` is read as the start of a specifier, so `"50%".formatted()` throws at run time. Write `%%` instead. Because `println` ends the line for you, the format string does not need `%n` here.

example.title: City labels
example.prompt: Build one label with String.format and another with formatted, then print both.
example.output:
Lisbon had 1,234,567 visitors this year
Save 15% today, rated 4.6 stars
example.explanation: `String.format` fills `%s` with the city and `%,d` with the visitor count, adding commas. `formatted` works the same way but is called on the format string. In `"Save %d%% today"` the `%d` prints `15` and `%%` prints `%`, and `%.1f` rounds the rating to one decimal.

practice.title: Sales summary
practice.prompt:
Build and print a two line sales summary.

1. Build `summary` with `formatted` so it reads `North sales: 2,480,000 dollars, up 12.4%`. Use `%s`, `%,d`, and `%.1f%%`.
2. Build `orderLine` with `String.format` so it reads `Orders: 15,320`.
3. Keep the two `println` calls from the starter.

Expected output:

```text
North sales: 2,480,000 dollars, up 12.4%
Orders: 15,320
```
hints: Call `formatted` on the format string: `"%s sales: ...".formatted(region, revenue, growth)`.
To print `12.4%`, write `%.1f%%`: the first part formats the number, `%%` adds the percent sign.

recap:
- `"text " + value` turns the value into text and joins it.
- `+` runs left to right: `"Total: " + 1 + 2` is `Total: 12`, so write `(1 + 2)`.
- `printf` uses `%s`, `%d`, `%f`, `%.2f`, `%c`, `%b`, and ends lines with `%n`.
- `%5d` right-aligns in 5 columns and `%-8s` left-aligns in 8.
- `String.format(...)` and `"...".formatted(...)` return the text instead of printing it.
- `%,d` adds thousands separators and `%%` prints a percent sign.
- A wrong type, such as `%d` with a double, compiles but fails when it runs.
